1.  **Longest overall bridge (by total length):** The **Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge** in China is the longest bridge in the world by total length, spanning approximately 164.8 kilometers (102 miles). It was **completed in 2010** and **opened to traffic in 2011**.

2.  **Longest continuous bridge over water:** The **Lake Pontchartrain Causeway** in Louisiana, USA, holds the record for the longest continuous bridge over open water, stretching about 38.4 km (23.9 miles) across Lake Pontchartrain.

## “Bridge-spiration” proves what humans are capable of.
During the current global health crisis, few people are thinking big. It’s a time when most are worried about simply making it through the day.
However, it’s important during times like these to think about what’s possible. That’s why we’re sharing our list of the world’s longest and most inspiring bridges and what makes them all so awesome.
We hope that it brightens your day and gets you thinking about what could be possible in the future.

## 1. The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge,China
This bridge was completed a decade ago in 2010 and opened in 2011. It has held the record for the world’s longest bridge ever since. The structure is a remarkable 102 miles long. It runs between Shanghai and Nanjing in the Jiangsu province, carrying the Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway across the Yangtze River delta, from Danyang to Kunshan. It is one of four Railway bridges that made it onto this list. The bridge took four years to build and cost between $8.5 and $10 billion, depending on the source. It required more than 10,000 people to get the work done.
**Awesomeness factor:**_The setting for this bridge is stunning, made up of lowland rice paddies, canals, rivers, and lakes. The bridge complements — or enhances — the natural vistas in the areas that it crosses. It makes for a train ride that people never forget._

## 2. Changhua–Kaohsiung Viaduct, China
This is currently the second longest bridge in the world. It carries part of the Taiwan High Speed Rail network. The bridge extends almost 98 miles from Banguashan in Changhua to Zuoying in Kaohsiung. It was completed in 2007.
**Awesomeness factor:**_Part of what makes this viaduct so unique is that it’s one of a series of bridges designed to be earthquake resistant. It allows for trains to stop safely during seismic events. The design also limits damage to individual sections of the viaduct so it can be repaired quickly after an earthquake._

## 3. Tianjin Grand Bridge, China
This railroad viaduct comes in at just over 70 miles long. It runs between Langfang and Qingxian, carrying the Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway. It’s the second of the four bridges on our list that are part of that rail system. Construction of it ended in 2010 after four years of work.
**Awesomeness factor:**_This may not be the most beautiful bridge on the list, but its structure is unique._ _It consists of a series of box girders, each more than 100 feet long, weighing 860 tons apiece. The girders were made in two workplaces along the bridge route, brought to where they needed to be installed, and then placed on piers already in place by a special crane. Lifts similar to those offered by__BridgeMasters__were used as part of the construction process._

## 4. Cangde Grand Bridge, China
This bridge, the world’s fourth longest, is the third on our list that’s part of the Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway. This bridge is almost 66 miles long and has a total of 3,092 piers.
**Awesomeness factor:**_The series of bridges that carry the railway line cut travel time across Hong Kong, Macau, and mainland China from three hours to just 30 minutes._

## 5. The Weinan Weihe Grand Bridge, China
This is another Chinese railway bridge that makes our list of the world’s longest viaducts. It’s part of the Zhengzhou-Xi’an High Speed Railway. It’s just under 50 miles long. It’s unusual because it crosses the Wei River twice, along with several other rivers, including the Ling, Luofu, Xi, and Shi Di. It was the longest bridge in the world for a short time after it was completed in 2008 and opened in 2010. However, it was quickly eclipsed by other bridges completed at the same time.
**Awesomeness factor:**_This viaduct is another major feat of engineering. There were more than 10,000 workers involved in its construction. It required upward of 2.3 million cubic meters of concrete and 45,000 tons of steel to be completed._

## 6. Bang Na Expressway, Thailand
At just over 34 miles long, this is the longest automotive viaduct on our list. Construction was completed in early 2000. It’s one of the few record- length bridges that does not cross a large water mass. It only transverses the Bang Pakong River for a short distance. It carries a six-lane elevated highway above another highway.
**Awesomeness factor:**_This is a utilitarian- looking structure, but it’s highway- over- highway design makes it unique and quite a feat of engineering._

## 7. Beijing Grand Bridge, China
At just under 30 miles long, this viaduct connects the two global business hubs of Beijing and Shanghai. It is the fourth bridge that’s part of the Beijing-–Shanghai High-Speed Railway to be on make our list. It was completed in 2010 and officially opened to rail traffic in 2011.
**Awesomeness factor:**_People taking trips on the Beijing-–Shanghai High-Speed Railway begin or end their journeys on this bridge. It is located just south of Beijing._

## 8. Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, United States
The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway is the longest bridge in the United States and the longest in the world that runs continuously over water. The causeway consists of two parallel bridges crossing Lake Pontchartrain in southern Louisiana. The longer of the two bridges is almost 24 miles in length. The first of the two bridges was completed in 1956. When traffic on it exceeded capacity, the second was added. Construction was finished, and it was opened to traffic in 1969.
**Awesomeness factor:**_The causeway has survived many hurricanes over the years, including Hurricane Katrina in 2005. During that major storm, the only damage to the structure was to a few turnarounds._

## 9. Line 1 (Wuhan Metro), China
Line 1 of the Wuhan Metro isn’t a bridge in the traditional sense. It’s actually the longest continuous metro system viaduct in the world. The entire line is almost 24 miles long and has 32 stations. It carries an elevated light rail line through Wuhan. It opened in 1995 and underwent renovations in 2003.
**Awesomeness factor:**_Line 1 is part of an extended train system that makes it easy for people to travel throughout Wuhan._

## 10. Manchac Swamp Bridge, United States
The Manchac Swamp Bridge is a twin concrete trestle structure located in the Lake Pontchartrain area of Louisiana. At almost 23 miles long, it is one of the longest bridges in the world built over water, along with being the longest on the United States Interstate Highway System. The bridge opened in 1979. Piles had to be driven more than 250 feet below a swamp to construct it. At the time, it cost $7 million per mile to complete.

Title: The Longest Bridges In The World That Cross Open Water
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
Imagine driving for miles and miles with nothing but water on either side. On Louisiana's Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, one eight-mile stretch puts drivers out of sight of land in every direction. Some bridges stretch more than 30 miles across open water. Crossing a small river is one thing, but stretching a road for dozens of miles across a coastal waterway is something entirely different. Bridges over open water are a remarkable feat of engineering, combining enormous lengths with carefully designed supports, artificial islands, tunnels, and sophisticated construction techniques. These are five of the most impressive bridges in the world, running from the longest down.

## Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge, China and Hong Kong
The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge across the Pearl River Estuary, the longest of these crossings at about 55 kilometers.
Completed in 2018, the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge is far more than a typical bridge. It is closer to a corridor across the water. Spanning the Pearl River Estuary, this monumental transportation system connects Hong Kong, Zhuhai, and Macau through a combination of bridges, tunnels, and artificial islands. This intricate system measures about 34 miles (55 kilometers) and includes bridges, viaducts, artificial islands, and an underwater tunnel. All of these elements make it one of the most ambitious infrastructure projects in the world. The bridge opened to public traffic in 2018 and dramatically reduced travel times between the three areas. What once could be a lengthy journey around the Pearl River Delta became a more direct connection.
Constructing the bridge was no easy task. Engineers had to work around busy shipping routes, powerful currents, typhoons, and marine ecosystems, all in the middle of one of the world's most developed coastal areas. The underwater tunnel is a fascinating detail, with engineers creating an approximately 6.7-kilometer tunnel immersed beneath the estuary. This preserved a navigation route for large, important ships while allowing the crossing to continue uninterrupted. Additionally, artificial islands were built to connect the bridge sections to the tunnel and serve as essential transition points within the network.

## Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah Causeway, Kuwait
Kuwait's Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah Causeway opened on May 1, 2019, and it crosses Kuwait Bay in two directions rather than one. The combined length reaches 30.1 miles (48.5 kilometers), divided between a Main Link running north from Kuwait City toward the Subiya region and a shorter Doha Link heading west. Nearly 80% of that length is offshore. The project was designed by the French engineering group Systra and cost around $3.6 billion. It was built by a consortium led by South Korea's Hyundai Engineering and Construction.
Reaching Subiya once meant a journey of roughly a 90-minute drive around the coast. The causeway cut that to about 30 minutes. There are two artificial islands out in the middle of the bay, with maintenance buildings, fuel stations, and marina facilities. The centerpiece is a cable-stayed span with a sail-shaped pylon rising nearly 500 feet above the water. Its navigation channel is wide and high enough for ships heading to port. Engineers even sank 1,000 rocks and reef blocks into the bay to replace habitat disturbed during construction.

## Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge, Shandong Province, China
China is home to some of the world's most ambitious bridge projects, and the spectacular Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge, which opened in June 2011 after four years of construction, is no exception. Located in Shandong Province, the bridge itself runs 16.6 miles (26.7 kilometers), almost all of it over water. The wider connection project it belongs to, which folds in expressways and an undersea tunnel, reaches an astounding 25.84 miles (41.58 kilometers) in aggregated length. Aggregated length means Qingdao has different bridge and road sections added together, unlike the continuous bridge of the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway. On that aggregated figure, the Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge has held a Guinness World Record for the longest bridge over water, revealing that the title of longest bridge can depend on how length is measured.
It crosses Jiaozhou Bay and was designed to improve transportation around the rapidly developing Qingdao region. Before it was built, traveling around the bay would require a much longer road journey, so the connection created a convenient direct route between parts of the city and surrounding communities.

## Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, Louisiana, United States
The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana, which holds the record for the longest continuous bridge over water.
The extraordinary Lake Pontchartrain Causeway stretches 23.83 miles (38.35 kilometers) across Lake Pontchartrain in Louisiana and holds a Guinness World Record for the longest continuous bridge over water. The original causeway opened in 1956, and a second adjacent span was completed in 1969. It is made of two parallel concrete bridges running between the lake's north and south shores, providing a vital connection between busy New Orleans and many communities to the north.
For roughly eight miles, the causeway becomes so isolated that drivers can lose sight of land entirely. Looking in almost every direction, there is nothing but water and sky. The experience can feel like traveling out into the middle of the sea. The length makes maintenance a formidable undertaking however, because engineers must contend with unpredictable weather, wind, waves, corrosion, and constant vehicle movement. What looks like a simple straight line across the water is actually a massive piece of infrastructure requiring continual inspection and upkeep.

## Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel, Virginia, United States
The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel connects Virginia Beach with the state's Eastern Shore.
Opened in 1964, the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel runs for approximately 17.6 miles (28.3 kilometers) across the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia, connecting Virginia Beach with the Eastern Shore. It combines trestle bridges, artificial islands, and underwater tunnels instead of rising continuously above the water. The tunnel sections are necessary because the Chesapeake Bay is a busy shipping route, and building a bridge high enough for large ships to pass beneath would create major engineering and navigational challenges. Instead, the roadway descends below the water's surface, passes through a tunnel, and then emerges above again.
Between the tunnels are artificial islands that serve as transition points. From a driver's perspective, the experience can seem almost surreal. One moment the road runs above open water, then it drops below the surface and into a tunnel, only to emerge onto another bridge. Ultimately it represents a unique approach to overcoming the basic obstacles of getting people and vehicles across a huge expanse of water.

## Bridging the Impossible
These bridges cross open water in very different ways. Lake Pontchartrain stretches continuously over water without touching land or entering a tunnel. Qingdao combines a long bridge with expressways and an undersea tunnel. The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel is shorter, but part of its route drops below the surface.
Each structure solves a different engineering problem. Shipping lanes need to stay open, storms put huge forces on exposed spans, and salt water constantly wears at concrete and steel. Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau uses a tunnel beneath the estuary, and Kuwait built artificial islands to support its crossing. From above, they may look like simple lines across the water, but each one required years of planning and major engineering decisions to turn open water into a highway.

O n our travels, we cross long and tall ones.**Bridges**, especially**road bridges**, are part of the landscape that we consider common when we go along roads tens of metres above a river or a valley. In some cases, however, we are dealing with engineering work that, in terms of their size and technical aspects, leaves us speechless. Think of the**Millau Viaduct in France**, which boasts a height of 341 metres, or the**Beipanjiang bridge in China**, which stands 565 metres above the Beipan River.
**Sometimes**it is not the height of the bridge**that amaze us**, but rather**their length**.**In Italy,**for example,**the record goes to the Coltano viaduct on the A12 motorway, which extends for 9.6 kilometres. In second place**in our country,**is the viaduct on the A19 motorway, which crosses the Fichera stream at a length of seven kilometres.**
But**the longest bridge in the world**boasts even more noteworthy dimensions: in fact, it reaches an extension of**164,800 metres**, more than the distance between Bari and Lecce in Italy.
**Where is the longest bridge in the world?**And how long are the other viaducts that stand out by extension?

#### 1. Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge
**Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge**– With the aforementioned**164,800 metres in length**, this viaduct wins the title for**the longest bridge in the world.**Its construction began in 2006 and, employing over 10,000 people, was completed in 2010 at a**total cost of $8.5 billion.**Such an incredibly long bridge was necessary to cross an area dotted with canals, rivers, lakes and rice fields. As part of the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed rail line,**the longest bridge in the world is located between Shanghai and Nanjing in Jiangsu province.**For nine kilometres, it passes over the waters of the Yangcheng lake.

#### 2. Changhua-Koahsiung Viaduct
**Changhua-Koahsiung Viaduct –****The second**longest bridge in the world is located in Taiwan, and is about seven kilometres shorter than the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge.**The Changhua-Koahsiung viaduct is 157,317 metres long**and is a key part of the Taiwan High -Speed Rail line. Completed in 2007, this bridge –**given the particular geographical area**between Baguazhang and Zuoying –**was built following strict anti-seismic criteria.**

#### 3. Cangde Grand Bridge
**Cangde Grand Bridge**–**Cangde Grand Bridge**is third place at**115,900 metres.**This bridge, like the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge, is also located along the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed line.**The viaduct has a total of 3,092 pillars**and was completed in 2010, the same year as the largest bridge in the world.

#### 4. Tianjin Grand Bridge
**Tianjin Grand Bridge**– Even**the fourth longest bridge in the world is located in Asia**, again in China, and always on the railway network. Altogether**113,700 metres long**, it extends between Langfang and Qingxian. Work began in 2006 and ended in 2010. The bridge was inaugurated in 2011.

#### 5. Weinan Weihe Grand Bridge
**Weinan Weihe Grand Bridge**– We remain in China even for**fifth**place but this structure is detached from the extensions of the previously mentioned viaducts.**The Weinan Weihe Grand Bridge**is in fact**79,732 metres long.**Its construction ended in 2008, so as to conquer – albeit briefly – the title of the longest bridge in the world. This viaduct is part of the Zhengzhou – Xi’an High-Speed Railway.

#### 6. Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge
**Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge**– In**sixth position**there is a**new entry,**the**Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao bridge, opened in 2018.**This structure connects Hong Kong, Zhuhai and Macao – the most important cities of the delta of the Pearl River – crossing the Lingdingyang canal. Some**55,717 metres in length**, the bridge was completed in 2017 after eight years of work. Some interesting data: the bridge was built using 400,000 tonnes of steel and has an underwater tunnel nearly seven kilometres long. The cost of the entire work, although unofficial, was about $7 billion. One last**curiosity**about this new entry:**the shape of the bridge is reminiscent of the typical Chinese dragon.**

#### 7. Bang Na Expressway
**Bang Na Expressway**–**Seventh place**in the ranking is awarded to a bridge that is located in Thailand. It**is 54 kilometres long**, so slightly less than the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge. Except for the crossing of a river, the railway viaduct rises over kilometres and kilometres of dry land. Designed in 1994 by Louis Berger, the bridge**was completed in 2000. ## “Bridge-spiration” proves what humans are capable of.
During the current global health crisis, few people are thinking big. It’s a time when most are worried about simply making it through the day.
However, it’s important during times like these to think about what’s possible. That’s why we’re sharing our list of the world’s longest and most inspiring bridges and what makes them all so awesome.
We hope that it brightens your day and gets you thinking about what could be possible in the future.
texts.1:
## 1. The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge,China
This bridge was completed a decade ago in 2010 and opened in 2011. It has held the record for the world’s longest bridge ever since. The structure is a remarkable 102 miles long. It runs between Shanghai and Nanjing in the Jiangsu province, carrying the Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway across the Yangtze River delta, from Danyang to Kunshan. It is one of four Railway bridges that made it onto this list. The bridge took four years to build and cost between $8.5 and $10 billion, depending on the source. It required more than 10,000 people to get the work done.
**Awesomeness factor:**_The setting for this bridge is stunning, made up of lowland rice paddies, canals, rivers, and lakes. The bridge complements — or enhances — the natural vistas in the areas that it crosses. It makes for a train ride that people never forget._
texts.2:
## 2. Changhua–Kaohsiung Viaduct, China
This is currently the second longest bridge in the world. It carries part of the Taiwan High Speed Rail network. The bridge extends almost 98 miles from Banguashan in Changhua to Zuoying in Kaohsiung. It was completed in 2007.
**Awesomeness factor:**_Part of what makes this viaduct so unique is that it’s one of a series of bridges designed to be earthquake resistant. It allows for trains to stop safely during seismic events. The design also limits damage to individual sections of the viaduct so it can be repaired quickly after an earthquake._
texts.3:
## 3. Tianjin Grand Bridge, China
This railroad viaduct comes in at just over 70 miles long. It runs between Langfang and Qingxian, carrying the Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway. It’s the second of the four bridges on our list that are part of that rail system. Construction of it ended in 2010 after four years of work.
**Awesomeness factor:**_This may not be the most beautiful bridge on the list, but its structure is unique._ _It consists of a series of box girders, each more than 100 feet long, weighing 860 tons apiece. The girders were made in two workplaces along the bridge route, brought to where they needed to be installed, and then placed on piers already in place by a special crane. Lifts similar to those offered by__BridgeMasters__were used as part of the construction process._
texts.4:
## 4. Cangde Grand Bridge, China
This bridge, the world’s fourth longest, is the third on our list that’s part of the Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway. This bridge is almost 66 miles long and has a total of 3,092 piers.
**Awesomeness factor:**_The series of bridges that carry the railway line cut travel time across Hong Kong, Macau, and mainland China from three hours to just 30 minutes._
texts.5:
## 5. The Weinan Weihe Grand Bridge, China
This is another Chinese railway bridge that makes our list of the world’s longest viaducts. It’s part of the Zhengzhou-Xi’an High Speed Railway. It’s just under 50 miles long. It’s unusual because it crosses the Wei River twice, along with several other rivers, including the Ling, Luofu, Xi, and Shi Di. It was the longest bridge in the world for a short time after it was completed in 2008 and opened in 2010. However, it was quickly eclipsed by other bridges completed at the same time.
**Awesomeness factor:**_This viaduct is another major feat of engineering. There were more than 10,000 workers involved in its construction. It required upward of 2.3 million cubic meters of concrete and 45,000 tons of steel to be completed._
texts.6:
## 6. Bang Na Expressway, Thailand
At just over 34 miles long, this is the longest automotive viaduct on our list. Construction was completed in early 2000. It’s one of the few record- length bridges that does not cross a large water mass. It only transverses the Bang Pakong River for a short distance. It carries a six-lane elevated highway above another highway.
**Awesomeness factor:**_This is a utilitarian- looking structure, but it’s highway- over- highway design makes it unique and quite a feat of engineering._
texts.7:
## 7. Beijing Grand Bridge, China
At just under 30 miles long, this viaduct connects the two global business hubs of Beijing and Shanghai. It is the fourth bridge that’s part of the Beijing-–Shanghai High-Speed Railway to be on make our list. It was completed in 2010 and officially opened to rail traffic in 2011.
**Awesomeness factor:**_People taking trips on the Beijing-–Shanghai High-Speed Railway begin or end their journeys on this bridge. It is located just south of Beijing._

## 8. Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, United States
The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway is the longest bridge in the United States and the longest in the world that runs continuously over water. The causeway consists of two parallel bridges crossing Lake Pontchartrain in southern Louisiana. The longer of the two bridges is almost 24 miles in length. The first of the two bridges was completed in 1956. When traffic on it exceeded capacity, the second was added. Construction was finished, and it was opened to traffic in 1969.
**Awesomeness factor:**_The causeway has survived many hurricanes over the years, including Hurricane Katrina in 2005. During that major storm, the only damage to the structure was to a few turnarounds._

**Awesomeness factor:**_Line 1 is part of an extended train system that makes it easy for people to travel throughout Wuhan._

texts.0: Imagine driving for miles and miles with nothing but water on either side. On Louisiana's Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, one eight-mile stretch puts drivers out of sight of land in every direction. Some bridges stretch more than 30 miles across open water. Crossing a small river is one thing, but stretching a road for dozens of miles across a coastal waterway is something entirely different. Bridges over open water are a remarkable feat of engineering, combining enormous lengths with carefully designed supports, artificial islands, tunnels, and sophisticated construction techniques. These are five of the most impressive bridges in the world, running from the longest down.
texts.1:
## Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge, China and Hong Kong
The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge across the Pearl River Estuary, the longest of these crossings at about 55 kilometers.
Completed in 2018, the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge is far more than a typical bridge. It is closer to a corridor across the water. Spanning the Pearl River Estuary, this monumental transportation system connects Hong Kong, Zhuhai, and Macau through a combination of bridges, tunnels, and artificial islands. This intricate system measures about 34 miles (55 kilometers) and includes bridges, viaducts, artificial islands, and an underwater tunnel. All of these elements make it one of the most ambitious infrastructure projects in the world. The bridge opened to public traffic in 2018 and dramatically reduced travel times between the three areas. What once could be a lengthy journey around the Pearl River Delta became a more direct connection.
Constructing the bridge was no easy task. Engineers had to work around busy shipping routes, powerful currents, typhoons, and marine ecosystems, all in the middle of one of the world's most developed coastal areas. The underwater tunnel is a fascinating detail, with engineers creating an approximately 6.7-kilometer tunnel immersed beneath the estuary. This preserved a navigation route for large, important ships while allowing the crossing to continue uninterrupted. Additionally, artificial islands were built to connect the bridge sections to the tunnel and serve as essential transition points within the network.
texts.2:
## Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah Causeway, Kuwait
Kuwait's Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah Causeway opened on May 1, 2019, and it crosses Kuwait Bay in two directions rather than one. The combined length reaches 30.1 miles (48.5 kilometers), divided between a Main Link running north from Kuwait City toward the Subiya region and a shorter Doha Link heading west. Nearly 80% of that length is offshore. The project was designed by the French engineering group Systra and cost around $3.6 billion. It was built by a consortium led by South Korea's Hyundai Engineering and Construction.
Reaching Subiya once meant a journey of roughly a 90-minute drive around the coast. The causeway cut that to about 30 minutes. There are two artificial islands out in the middle of the bay, with maintenance buildings, fuel stations, and marina facilities. The centerpiece is a cable-stayed span with a sail-shaped pylon rising nearly 500 feet above the water. Its navigation channel is wide and high enough for ships heading to port. Engineers even sank 1,000 rocks and reef blocks into the bay to replace habitat disturbed during construction.
texts.3:
## Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge, Shandong Province, China
China is home to some of the world's most ambitious bridge projects, and the spectacular Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge, which opened in June 2011 after four years of construction, is no exception. Located in Shandong Province, the bridge itself runs 16.6 miles (26.7 kilometers), almost all of it over water. The wider connection project it belongs to, which folds in expressways and an undersea tunnel, reaches an astounding 25.84 miles (41.58 kilometers) in aggregated length. Aggregated length means Qingdao has different bridge and road sections added together, unlike the continuous bridge of the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway. On that aggregated figure, the Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge has held a Guinness World Record for the longest bridge over water, revealing that the title of longest bridge can depend on how length is measured.
It crosses Jiaozhou Bay and was designed to improve transportation around the rapidly developing Qingdao region. Before it was built, traveling around the bay would require a much longer road journey, so the connection created a convenient direct route between parts of the city and surrounding communities.
texts.4:
## Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, Louisiana, United States
The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana, which holds the record for the longest continuous bridge over water.
The extraordinary Lake Pontchartrain Causeway stretches 23.83 miles (38.35 kilometers) across Lake Pontchartrain in Louisiana and holds a Guinness World Record for the longest continuous bridge over water. The original causeway opened in 1956, and a second adjacent span was completed in 1969. It is made of two parallel concrete bridges running between the lake's north and south shores, providing a vital connection between busy New Orleans and many communities to the north.
For roughly eight miles, the causeway becomes so isolated that drivers can lose sight of land entirely. Looking in almost every direction, there is nothing but water and sky. The experience can feel like traveling out into the middle of the sea. The length makes maintenance a formidable undertaking however, because engineers must contend with unpredictable weather, wind, waves, corrosion, and constant vehicle movement. What looks like a simple straight line across the water is actually a massive piece of infrastructure requiring continual inspection and upkeep.
texts.5:
## Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel, Virginia, United States
The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel connects Virginia Beach with the state's Eastern Shore.
Opened in 1964, the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel runs for approximately 17.6 miles (28.3 kilometers) across the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia, connecting Virginia Beach with the Eastern Shore. It combines trestle bridges, artificial islands, and underwater tunnels instead of rising continuously above the water. The tunnel sections are necessary because the Chesapeake Bay is a busy shipping route, and building a bridge high enough for large ships to pass beneath would create major engineering and navigational challenges. Instead, the roadway descends below the water's surface, passes through a tunnel, and then emerges above again.
Between the tunnels are artificial islands that serve as transition points. From a driver's perspective, the experience can seem almost surreal. One moment the road runs above open water, then it drops below the surface and into a tunnel, only to emerge onto another bridge. Ultimately it represents a unique approach to overcoming the basic obstacles of getting people and vehicles across a huge expanse of water.
texts.6:
## Bridging the Impossible
These bridges cross open water in very different ways. Lake Pontchartrain stretches continuously over water without touching land or entering a tunnel. Qingdao combines a long bridge with expressways and an undersea tunnel. The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel is shorter, but part of its route drops below the surface.
Each structure solves a different engineering problem. Shipping lanes need to stay open, storms put huge forces on exposed spans, and salt water constantly wears at concrete and steel. Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau uses a tunnel beneath the estuary, and Kuwait built artificial islands to support its crossing. From above, they may look like simple lines across the water, but each one required years of planning and major engineering decisions to turn open water into a highway.

Imagine driving for miles and miles with nothing but water on either side. On Louisiana's Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, one eight-mile stretch puts drivers out of sight of land in every direction. Some bridges stretch more than 30 miles across open water. Crossing a small river is one thing, but stretching a road for dozens of miles across a coastal waterway is something entirely different. Bridges over open water are a remarkable feat of engineering, combining enormous lengths with carefully designed supports, artificial islands, tunnels, and sophisticated construction techniques. These are five of the most impressive bridges in the world, running from the longest down.

## Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge, China and Hong Kong
The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge across the Pearl River Estuary, the longest of these crossings at about 55 kilometers.
Completed in 2018, the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge is far more than a typical bridge. It is closer to a corridor across the water. Spanning the Pearl River Estuary, this monumental transportation system connects Hong Kong, Zhuhai, and Macau through a combination of bridges, tunnels, and artificial islands. This intricate system measures about 34 miles (55 kilometers) and includes bridges, viaducts, artificial islands, and an underwater tunnel. All of these elements make it one of the most ambitious infrastructure projects in the world. The bridge opened to public traffic in 2018 and dramatically reduced travel times between the three areas. What once could be a lengthy journey around the Pearl River Delta became a more direct connection.
Constructing the bridge was no easy task. Engineers had to work around busy shipping routes, powerful currents, typhoons, and marine ecosystems, all in the middle of one of the world's most developed coastal areas. The underwater tunnel is a fascinating detail, with engineers creating an approximately 6.7-kilometer tunnel immersed beneath the estuary. This preserved a navigation route for large, important ships while allowing the crossing to continue uninterrupted. Additionally, artificial islands were built to connect the bridge sections to the tunnel and serve as essential transition points within the network.

## Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah Causeway, Kuwait
Kuwait's Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah Causeway opened on May 1, 2019, and it crosses Kuwait Bay in two directions rather than one. The combined length reaches 30.1 miles (48.5 kilometers), divided between a Main Link running north from Kuwait City toward the Subiya region and a shorter Doha Link heading west. Nearly 80% of that length is offshore. The project was designed by the French engineering group Systra and cost around $3.6 billion. It was built by a consortium led by South Korea's Hyundai Engineering and Construction.
Reaching Subiya once meant a journey of roughly a 90-minute drive around the coast. The causeway cut that to about 30 minutes. There are two artificial islands out in the middle of the bay, with maintenance buildings, fuel stations, and marina facilities. The centerpiece is a cable-stayed span with a sail-shaped pylon rising nearly 500 feet above the water. Its navigation channel is wide and high enough for ships heading to port. Engineers even sank 1,000 rocks and reef blocks into the bay to replace habitat disturbed during construction.

## Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge, Shandong Province, China
China is home to some of the world's most ambitious bridge projects, and the spectacular Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge, which opened in June 2011 after four years of construction, is no exception. Located in Shandong Province, the bridge itself runs 16.6 miles (26.7 kilometers), almost all of it over water. The wider connection project it belongs to, which folds in expressways and an undersea tunnel, reaches an astounding 25.84 miles (41.58 kilometers) in aggregated length. Aggregated length means Qingdao has different bridge and road sections added together, unlike the continuous bridge of the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway. On that aggregated figure, the Qingdao Jiaozhou Bay Bridge has held a Guinness World Record for the longest bridge over water, revealing that the title of longest bridge can depend on how length is measured.
It crosses Jiaozhou Bay and was designed to improve transportation around the rapidly developing Qingdao region. Before it was built, traveling around the bay would require a much longer road journey, so the connection created a convenient direct route between parts of the city and surrounding communities.

## Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, Louisiana, United States
The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana, which holds the record for the longest continuous bridge over water.
The extraordinary Lake Pontchartrain Causeway stretches 23.83 miles (38.35 kilometers) across Lake Pontchartrain in Louisiana and holds a Guinness World Record for the longest continuous bridge over water. The original causeway opened in 1956, and a second adjacent span was completed in 1969. It is made of two parallel concrete bridges running between the lake's north and south shores, providing a vital connection between busy New Orleans and many communities to the north.
For roughly eight miles, the causeway becomes so isolated that drivers can lose sight of land entirely. Looking in almost every direction, there is nothing but water and sky. The experience can feel like traveling out into the middle of the sea. The length makes maintenance a formidable undertaking however, because engineers must contend with unpredictable weather, wind, waves, corrosion, and constant vehicle movement. What looks like a simple straight line across the water is actually a massive piece of infrastructure requiring continual inspection and upkeep.

## Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel, Virginia, United States
The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel connects Virginia Beach with the state's Eastern Shore.
Opened in 1964, the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel runs for approximately 17.6 miles (28.3 kilometers) across the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia, connecting Virginia Beach with the Eastern Shore. It combines trestle bridges, artificial islands, and underwater tunnels instead of rising continuously above the water. The tunnel sections are necessary because the Chesapeake Bay is a busy shipping route, and building a bridge high enough for large ships to pass beneath would create major engineering and navigational challenges. Instead, the roadway descends below the water's surface, passes through a tunnel, and then emerges above again.
Between the tunnels are artificial islands that serve as transition points. From a driver's perspective, the experience can seem almost surreal. One moment the road runs above open water, then it drops below the surface and into a tunnel, only to emerge onto another bridge. Ultimately it represents a unique approach to overcoming the basic obstacles of getting people and vehicles across a huge expanse of water.

## Bridging the Impossible
These bridges cross open water in very different ways. Lake Pontchartrain stretches continuously over water without touching land or entering a tunnel. Qingdao combines a long bridge with expressways and an undersea tunnel. The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel is shorter, but part of its route drops below the surface.
Each structure solves a different engineering problem. Shipping lanes need to stay open, storms put huge forces on exposed spans, and salt water constantly wears at concrete and steel. Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau uses a tunnel beneath the estuary, and Kuwait built artificial islands to support its crossing. From above, they may look like simple lines across the water, but each one required years of planning and major engineering decisions to turn open water into a highway.

1.  **Longest overall bridge (by total length):** The **Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge** in China is the longest bridge in the world by total length, spanning approximately 164.8 kilometers (102 miles). It was **completed in 2010** and **opened to traffic in 2011**.

2.  **Longest continuous bridge over water:** The **Lake Pontchartrain Causeway** in Louisiana, USA, holds the record for the longest continuous bridge over open water, stretching about 38.4 km (23.9 miles) across Lake Pontchartrain.
    *   The first span of the causeway **opened in 1956**.
    *   A second parallel span was added later, with construction finishing and it opening to traffic in **1969**.
    *   While both spans exist today, the original 1956 opening established its status as the world's longest bridge over water at that time, a record it still holds for the continuous span over water specifically.

**Summary:**
*   If you mean the **absolute longest bridge ever built** (the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge), it opened in **2011**.
*   If you mean the **longest bridge over water** (the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway), the first part opened in **1956**, with the full double-span system completed/opening in **1969**.
